title: Larkfield DC: robot collision stops tripled in September
setting: Larkfield Distribution Centre is a fictional regional warehouse run by Corrin Freight Logistics. It operates 58 Halvane HR-7 autonomous mobile robots. Thirty-eight pallet-handling robots work the outbound marshalling Zones A and B, where wrapped outbound pallets are staged. Twenty tote robots work carton Zone C. A robot logs a 'collision stop' (protective stop) whenever an obstacle enters its protective field. The analysis date is 20 October 2026.
presentingRequest: The regional operations director writes: 'Larkfield's robot collision stops have roughly tripled since early September, in the middle of peak season. The GM wants a disciplinary policy for agency temps, and Halvane suggests shortening the robots' protective fields. Tell me what is actually driving the stops and what the site should do now.'

initialEvidence.source: Fleet management system, weekly safety KPI extract
initialEvidence.text: Larkfield DC: protective ('collision') stops, all 58 HR-7 robots, by ISO week 2026: wk30 201, wk31 209, wk32 198, wk33 212, wk34 207, wk35 203, wk36 412, wk37 640, wk38 655, wk39 662, wk40 648, wk41 651. A stop is logged whenever an obstacle enters a robot's protective field; the robot halts until the field clears, typically for 20–90 seconds. Physical contacts with people or equipment: 1 in weeks 30–35, 1 in weeks 37–41. Robot operating hours were roughly constant across the period.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Dana Okafor, General Manager, to site leadership, 5 October
initialEvidence.text: Subject: Robot stops. 'The timing tells the story. We brought in 46 agency temps on 31 August and the stops tripled that same week. These people don't know the lane rules and they wander into robot aisles. I want a three-strike policy live by Monday. Every collision stop gets matched to the temps rostered in that zone during that hour, each match counts as a strike, and after three strikes the agency replaces the person. Engineering keeps telling me it's the software, but Halvane says their update runs fine at other sites, so let's stop chasing that.'

Fleet firmware upgrade, HR-7 6.3 to 6.4. Implemented 2–4 September 2026 on 50 of 58 robots. Exception: eight pallet-handling robots with the older battery module (units P31–P38) stay on 6.3 until a compatible module arrives. They continue in normal mixed duty. Vendor release summary: 'Revised near-field return filtering for improved detection of low-profile obstacles; navigation and charging fixes; security patches.' Halvane lifecycle notice: security support for 6.3 ends 31 October 2026. The eight exception units are covered by a time-limited waiver.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Halvane Robotics Customer Support (Tier 2), 25 September
initialEvidence.text: 'We've reviewed your ticket. Firmware 6.4 has been live at three other customer sites since July with no change in protective-stop rates, so we don't see the firmware as the cause. Increases like this are usually environmental: people, layout, clutter. If the stops are hurting throughput, a common remedy is to shorten the protective field by 20%, and we can push that profile to your fleet remotely. Our next release, 6.4.2, is planned for early December and includes further filtering refinements.'

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, R. Szabo, robot maintenance technician, 12 October
initialEvidence.text: 'Most of the stops I get called out to are in the marshalling lanes, A and B, where outbound pallets are staged. There are hardly any in C, the tote zone. Usually by the time I get there the field's clear and nobody's around, but people walk off, so I can't say who it was. Somebody asked me about the new shiny pallet wrap; procurement switched suppliers at the start of August. I don't buy it. We had that wrap for a month before the stops went up and nothing changed. If it was the wrap, August would have been bad too.'

Missed carrier cut-offs averaged 2 per week in weeks 30–35 and 9 per week in weeks 37–41. Outbound pallet volume has been up 18% since week 35 as the seasonal peak ramped. Comparison row for the same weeks in 2025: cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week during that peak, while collision stops stayed near 200 per week. Dashboard note: robot stop time is not linked to wave completion data.

catalogue.title: Collision-stop event log with badge-tag proximity field, weeks 30–41
catalogue.source: Fleet management system export with HR roster note
catalogue.text: Each stop record shows the nearest UWB badge tag within 3 m at the moment of the stop. All floor staff and forklifts carry tags. Weekly averages: stops with a tag nearby were 41 in weeks 30–35 and 44 in weeks 37–41. Stops with no tag nearby were 164 in weeks 30–35 and 607 in weeks 37–41. September gate audits found 99.2% of floor entries tagged, agency temps included; temps receive tags at induction. HR roster note: from 31 August the 46 temps were spread across zones roughly in proportion to headcount: Zone A 17, Zone B 15, Zone C 14.

catalogue.title: Collision-stop rates by firmware group and zone, weeks 33–41
catalogue.source: Site engineering analysis of fleet telemetry
catalogue.text: Stops per 100 robot-hours, weeks 33–35 compared with weeks 37–41. Week 36 is excluded as the rollout week. Pallet robots upgraded to 6.4 in Zones A/B (30 units): 3.2 to 15.6. Pallet robots kept on 6.3 in Zones A/B (units P31–P38): 3.1 to 3.3. Tote robots upgraded to 6.4 in Zone C (20 units): 2.4 to 2.5. Mission assignment in A/B is dynamic and ignores firmware version. P31–P38 logged 21% of A/B robot-hours both before and after, on all three shifts, in line with their share of the units (8 of 38). Zone C handles cartons in open totes, and no stretch-wrapped pallets are staged there.

catalogue.title: Bench test of protective stops against staged outbound pallets, 14 October
catalogue.source: Test record co-signed by site engineering lead and Halvane field engineer
catalogue.text: Setup: one HR-7 driven past a row of staged outbound pallets at 0.6 m/s, at approach angles of 20–50° to the pallet face, 20 passes per condition, with no people in the area. Protective stops: firmware 6.4 with current gloss film, 17/20; 6.3 with gloss film, 1/20; 6.4 with the previous supplier's matte film, 0/20; 6.3 with matte film, 0/20. Field engineer's note: 6.4 keeps weak short-range returns that 6.3 discarded, so that it can catch thin obstacles such as fork tines. At oblique angles the gloss film throws short specular returns that 6.4 now treats as an obstacle. Release 6.4.2 is intended to reclassify such returns but has not been tested against this film.

catalogue.title: Agency temp induction and safety-training records, August–September
catalogue.text: 46 agency temps were inducted 27–31 August. Induction included the 40-minute robot-lane safety module and a supervised floor walk. Completion: 46/46 for the module and 45/46 for the floor walk (one completed it on 2 September). The quiz pass mark is 80%, and the median score was 90%. Two temps received verbal reminders in September for crossing a lane outside a marked crossing. There are no other conduct records. The agency reports that 4 temps left by mid-October and were replaced through the same induction.

catalogue.title: Lidar window cleaning and calibration log, July–October
catalogue.text: Scanner windows on all 58 robots were cleaned weekly from July to October, except week 38, when cleaning slipped to the Monday of week 39. All monthly calibration checks passed within tolerance. Two scanner heads were replaced: P07 in July after impact damage and T12 in September for a connector fault. No changes were made to cleaning materials or procedure in the period.

catalogue.title: Wi-Fi access-point and fleet-server latency logs, weeks 30–41
catalogue.text: Median round-trip latency between robots and the fleet server was 18 ms, with a 99th percentile of 84 ms, unchanged across weeks 30–41. Access-point firmware was unchanged. Three brief outages occurred in week 34 (11 minutes in total) and none afterwards. Protective stops are computed on board each robot. A network loss triggers a separate 'comms hold' category, which averaged 6 per week throughout.

catalogue.title: Halvane statement on 6.4 stop rates at other customer sites
catalogue.text: Three customer sites have run 6.4 since July. Stops per 100 robot-hours before and after the upgrade: Site R 2.9 to 3.0, Site M 3.6 to 3.4, Site T 2.2 to 2.3. Site environments vary: R is a parcel sortation hub, M is a cold store and T is a spare-parts warehouse. Halvane does not collect data on customers' load types or packaging. 'We remain confident 6.4 performs as designed across varied environments.'

catalogue.title: Stretch film technical data sheets, current and previous supplier
catalogue.text: Current film, Pellucid ClearCast 20: cast stretch film, 20 µm, high clarity, gloss 90 GU at 45°, haze 0.8%, pre-stretch up to 250%. Recommended for retail-ready loads where labels must be scanned through the film. Previous film, Northmoor HandiBlown 23: blown stretch film, 23 µm, gloss 55 GU, haze 6%, pre-stretch up to 200%. Neither sheet says anything about compatibility with automated equipment.

catalogue.title: Procurement record for the outbound stretch film change, July–August
catalogue.text: A purchase change was approved on 28 July to switch outbound stretch film from Northmoor to Pellucid from 4 August, for a 6% unit-cost saving and better scanning through the film. All outbound wrappers were converted by 11 August. The Northmoor frame agreement stays active for two other company sites, and Larkfield can call off stock within three working days at the old price. No other packaging changes were made.

catalogue.title: Robot-related near-miss and contact incident reports, weeks 30–41
catalogue.text: Self-reported near-miss forms involving robots: 3 in weeks 30–35 and 4 in weeks 37–41, two of the latter filed by agency temps. Contact incidents: one in each period. In week 33 a robot nudged an empty pallet, and in week 39 a robot brushed a cage trolley. There were no injuries. The safety lead notes that reporting rates are typical for the site.

catalogue.title: Wave-level analysis of missed carrier cut-offs, weeks 37–41
catalogue.text: Of 45 missed cut-offs in weeks 37–41, 31 were on the two largest carriers' evening waves, which grew most with peak volume (+26%). Missed waves had more robot collision stops in the preceding two hours than on-time waves (median 61 against 49), but they were also the largest waves. Analyst's note: 'I have not yet tried to separate the volume effect from the stop effect, and robot wait time isn't recorded per wave.'

catalogue.title: Robot battery health telemetry, July–October
catalogue.text: Average battery state of health: 91% for robots with the new module and 84% for the older-module units P31–P38. No stops were attributed to low battery. Charging cycles per robot per day were stable at 3.1–3.4. Two chargers in Zone C were relocated in week 31, with no change in charge queue times. Halvane expects compatible replacement modules for P31–P38 in January.

catalogue.title: Warehouse lighting work orders, January–October
catalogue.text: High-bay LED replacement in Zone A was completed 15–19 June (week 25). Zone B replacement is scheduled for November. There have been no lighting changes in Zone C since 2024. Monthly emergency-lighting tests passed. Two dock-door light fittings in Zone B were repaired in September after a storm. No work orders mention robots.

catalogue.title: Site safety committee minutes, 8 October
catalogue.text: Item 3, vendor proposal to shorten the protective field by 20%: site risk assessment RA-114 sets the current field length as the minimum for mixed pedestrian and robot lanes at 1.2 m/s. A 20% cut would need a lower top speed or a full reassessment. The committee did not endorse the proposal. Item 4, the GM's three-strike proposal: the union representative objected that strikes would be assigned by matching rosters to stops, not by observed conduct. The item was referred to the GM for decision.

catalogue.title: Fleet configuration and map change history, July–October
catalogue.text: Map edits: two charging stations moved in Zone C in week 31. Speed limits were unchanged (1.2 m/s in A/B, 1.0 m/s in C). Protective field profiles have been unchanged since March 2025. Mission-priority and traffic rules were unchanged. Firmware events in the period: CHG-2026-0412 only. No configuration rollbacks were recorded.

hypotheses.text: The September fleet firmware update, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
The August change of outbound pallet stretch film, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
Seasonal agency temps entering robot lanes caused the rise in collision stops.
The September firmware update and the August film change together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
The September firmware update and the arrival of the agency temps together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
Halvane's planned December release would, on its own, bring stop rates back to the pre-September level while the current film stays in use.

edges.from: Fleet firmware update from 6.3 to 6.4 (2–4 September)
Switch to the new outbound stretch film (August)
Arrival of 46 agency temps on the floor (31 August)

actions.text: Switch outbound pallets back to the previous supplier's stretch film, keep all robots on their current firmware, and track weekly stop rates by zone and firmware group against the September–October figures.
Roll the 30 upgraded pallet-handling robots back to firmware 6.3 under a temporary waiver until Halvane issues a corrected release, leaving the tote robots on 6.4.
Accept Halvane's offer to shorten the protective field by 20% on all robots to cut stop frequency during peak.
Introduce the GM's three-strike policy: match each collision stop to temps rostered in that zone and hour, and have the agency replace any temp who reaches three strikes.
Keep the current film and adopt Halvane's planned December release as the permanent fix, scheduling fleet-wide installation as soon as it ships.
